utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone and Happy New Year, a year in which we look forward to hard work in the next few months as we come to the end of this 18-month, I think they said, case. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian, Joanna Korner and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution. Happy New Year, indeed, to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Monika Marekova, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Happy New Year to everybody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, I don't know if the parties have any matters to raise, but the Chamber has a brief decision as follows: The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution was ordered to file its final version of the CHS database concerning the deaths of alleged victims by today. In view of the Prosecution's latest motion on this issue, the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecution an extension of this deadline until a time to be determined in the decision on the mentioned motion. In that decision, the Trial Chamber will further determine when the Defence should file its submissions on the final version of the CHS. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do have a custom matters to raise, if I may. The first is the question of the application to call further witnesses in rebuttal in respect of the Zupljanin case. Your Honours, the reason we ask for whether Your Honours are going to give a decision there week is twofold: Firstly, for planning purposes; and, secondly, I have spoken to Mr. Krgovic this morning, and in the light -- in the event that Your Honours do grand one or more, in particular our application to call an expert in rebuttal, they're going to be asking for three weeks, Your Honour, to prepare for the witnesses. So I'm wondering whether there's any prospect of there being a decision this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The short answer to that question is yes. It is a decision that we are top of and we appreciate the urgency of it, and, of course, what follows from that. Well, the scheduling will, of course, follow from any decision on scheduling -- would, of course, follow from what -- what the decision is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, because as I say, these the witnesses we're about to call are not likely to occupy more than this week, so that's the situation. Your Honour, the second matter is this: We applied for protective measures for the next witness. Your Honours, we really -- before I see him this afternoon, he really would like to know, and I would like to be able to tell him, whether his protective measures have been granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That decision is in the process of being filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I will be able to tell him that this afternoon, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, the protective measures have been granted and the decision, as I say, is in the process of being filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Those are the only matters that I wanted to raise then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, I would just like to raise one matter. I noticed from the -- from the announced documents of the Prosecutor for this witness that, at least in my opinion, three of the documents are clearly outside of the scope of the rebuttal testimony that this witness is allowed to give; specifically, documents tab 5, 7, and 8. And 5, 6, and 8, I'm sorry. 5, 6, and 8. And we'd kindly ask the explanation from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor because it will save time during the -- the testimony of the witness that I wouldn't need to object on presentation of these documents to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Let me deal with tab 5 to begin with. Tab 5 is a list of staff members working for the Doboj police in April of 1992. It is related to one of the topics that were granted in the decision relating to Mr. Bjelosevic's presence in Doboj during the month of May 1992. In there, there's a person that is listed and the Trial Chamber -- and the Defence, through Mr. Bjelosevic, challenged his presence in Doboj. And this was again dealt with in cross-examination with Mr. Radulovic. So through my questions, you will see that it is related to that topic of Mr. Bjelosevic's presence in Doboj in May of 1992. The second one is one of the -- I believe tab 6. Yes. Is one of the log-books of the central prison Doboj, just to corroborate the fact that the witness -- the next witness was detained there. Simply that his name appears in that log-book. It is it part of his testimony that he was arrested, et cetera. And following this release, he did see Mr. Bjelosevic. So it is part of that background of his testimony. And as of tab 8, this is a map of the 1st Krajina Corps indicating the area of responsibility of the corps. Actually, Your Honour, I may not use that one at all. It may be relevant to the next witness. So we'll see where we go with that one, but I don't believe that I will need to use it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't suppose that, Mr. Demirdjian, that you need to be reminded of the areas in respect of which this witness has been permitted to be called which is in the decision that we would have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there is nothing else, could the witness please be escorted into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you please read the solemn declaration on the card that the usher is now handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And please be seated. From your responses so far, I take it that you are hearing me in a language that you understand? Would you please confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as I said, welcome to the Tribunal, and you have been called by the Prosecution in terms of the -- their case in rebuttal of the case for the Defence. You would have begun by taking the solemn declaration which imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony, and should you give false or misleading testimony this Tribunal is empowered to deal with you as -- on -- on the -- for the offence of perjury under its statutes. The Prosecution, whose witness you are, has indicated that their examination-in-chief would take about two hours, and counsel for the second accused, I believe, have indicated a like period of time. The -- so your testimony should be completed within the course of today. The periods of sitting are of not more than an hour and a half duration because the -- because largely for technical reasons in terms of the tapes that have to be changed, so, therefore, the Court would take a break after -- 10.25 I think is the first break and resume in 20 minutes. But if you need, for whatever reason, to take a break other than that if you would indicate it to us and we would accommodate you. And with that, I would invite Mr. Demirdjian, who is counsel for the Prosecution, to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mirza Lisinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Kotorsko, Doboj municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you lived in the Doboj municipality all the way up to the war -- to the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to cover very quickly your educational background. Is it correct to say that you attended primary school and Gymnazijum in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I finished my elementary school in my native village and secondary school in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you graduated from the law faculty in Sarajevo in 1988?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Only the faculty had a branch in Doboj, but the degree itself was issued by the faculty in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Before I go through your professional background, can you tell us what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Over the last six or so years, I have been an employee of SIPA, the state agency for protection, and I was the internal control head, and that is the post that I have been holding since.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who appointed you to this position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there was an advertisement. This position was announced. But formally and officially, this decision was taken in September of 2005 by Mr. Paddy Ashdown, the administer, along with the staff from the administration, and a number of assistant directors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said you ended your studies in 1988. What -- did you start working immediately afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I started working in 1986, in Derventa, the social welfare centre. At the time, I had finished two years of the faculty of law. In 1998, I graduated, and before that, I did my military service. But as a lawyer, proper lawyer, I started in 1986 in the Doboj police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And were you appointed to a position in 1989?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: From 1989, the 1st of January, I became commander deputy of the Doboj police station, or the municipal SUP of Doboj. That is actually when I started working for the police as a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is correct to say that you held that position until the month of July in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, in the spring of that year, I became commander of the Doboj police station. The then-commander, Karlo Grgic, retired so I was the police station commander I think from April 1990 until July 1991. That would be the accurate state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. So first you were deputy commander and then you were promoted to commander. Now, in July 1991, was there someone who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: As a result, or a consequence of the first multi-party elections, new appointments were made in police so that as of July 1991, the police station commander was appointed, and that was Irfan Hadzic from Doboj, and I think he was a mechanical engineer. I remained in the station. I was not appointed to a new position, and I didn't receive any written decision. That means that I remained working until October 1991, which is the time when I received an official decision signed by Mr. Selimovic, the deputy of the republican secretary, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer, and, if possible, slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lisinovic, the interpreters are asking if you could possibly slow down and repeat the last part of your answer in relation to what you were doing after October 1991, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. It's slipped my mind. From October 1st, 1991, based on the decision issued by the Secretariat of the Interior of the republic based in Sarajevo, issued at the then-assistant secretary Selimovic, I was appointed to the CSB, specifically to the uniformed police section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the CSB had also gone through some changes that year. Who was the chief of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately at the time when these new appointments were made, Bogdan Nikolic was succeeded by Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic at the CSB; whereas in the public security station of Doboj, which is the municipal police, Milan Kovacevic was replaced by Obren Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned these new names, Irfan Hadzic, Andrija Bjelosevic and Obren Perovic, were these all political appointees?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Look, that was a time when people were flocking together on ethnic lines and bases, if I may describe it in that way. It was not strictly decided in that manner. These appointments were made by the secretariat in Sarajevo, but, nevertheless, without the political support of the ruling parties at the time, no one could become chief of police. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the former chief of police, Bogdan Nikolic, do you know what ethnicity he was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. And that is when he retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as of October 1991, you're working in this section in the CSB. Can you tell us exactly what your work entailed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: This section of the uniformed police, and there was also a criminal investigation section, my section actually had about two groups of workers. One of them were in charge of duty operations activities, working at the centre; and the other group was involved in directing and supervising the work of the police. And I was a member of this latter group, which means directing and supervising duties. We, who were involved in these kind of operations, had to perform some duty -- duty responsibilities in the event that someone was missing from the staff or absent for whatever reason. We were obliged to cover for them, although our decisions on appointment did not envisage this kind of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to clarify your position, you said that you were involved in directing and supervising the work of the police. Are we talking about only the municipal police here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So your work was limited to the Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. All the CSB responsibilities covered nine municipalities that were integral and constituent part of that centre, and the centre was actually the headquarters for the whole region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, who was your superior in this section?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Vojo Blagojevic was the chief of the uniformed police section at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: To Mr. Bjelosevic, the chief of the centre -- or, rather, I'm sorry, the centre had two sectors: The public security sector and the state security sector. That was a time when things functioned in that manner. There was no separate state security agency at the time. So we had a chief of the public security centre, or sector, so between the chief of the centre, you had the chief of the public security. At the time of these appointments, that position was occupied by Mr. Hodzic from Tesanj who was killed in a road accident, and then he was succeeded by Hasan Klokic. That was the public security sector; whereas, the state security sector was headed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, could you repeat the name of the head of the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Haso Klokic, can you tell us what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: A Bosniak, a Muslim. A Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And Ilija Bilic, what was his background?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe it is correct to say that in the CSB you also had a crime investigation department. Can you tell us who headed that unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that we had these two sections. Mr. Pejo Krnjic was the head of the criminal investigation section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you give us his ethnicity as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We've talked about the CSB. We've heard that there was an army barracks in Doboj. Can you tell us which units were located in Doboj? And I'm talking about the early part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Doboj had also had a garrison. It was a tradition where, of course, JNA troops were deployed, at the time when it existed as such. We had the barracks called the 4th of July, and there were a number of other smaller facilities in the surrounding villages, Sevarlije, Bare, et cetera, but mainly depots. So that all belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army because that was the only regular army at the time. Now, after its transformation into the Serbian army, when they removed these insignia, the situation changed since members of the Bosnian community abandoned and left the army, failed to respond to call-ups, et cetera, so effectively it became a Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And around which time would you say that this transformation took place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Already at the beginning of the conflict in Croatia is the time when these kind of changes were on the increase within the structure of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And in the garrison itself, do you know which unit, or which units were present, or were stationed there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did you know who was the commander of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: In the last half year that I worked at the centre, Cazim Hadzic, the lieutenant-general, was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, through your work, did you come to learn what influence he had over the activities of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not have proper access to the garrison; therefore, I cannot speak about how it operated. I had no access to this kind of information, and I had no access to the garrison itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you interact with any members of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: By the very nature of our job and as needed, we had certain contacts with the military security people, specifically with Captain Jeftic. I think that was his name. We had meetings with him, we co-operated with him, we were involved in some joint activities, et cetera. I think his last name was Jeftic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And through your interactions with Jeftic, did you learn about the situation in the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I really have to object now. The witness clearly explained that he doesn't have any knowledge whatsoever. So this is the second time that Mr. Demirdjian is trying to elicit answer from the witness where witness clearly said that he doesn't have any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe we'll be able to elicit this from the next question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lisinovic, did you know a man by the name of Milovan Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was a major. Everybody called him Major Stankovic. Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And your interactions with Captain Mr. Jeftic, did you come to learn of the relationship between Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to object against. First of all, the witness clearly said he doesn't have any information. He was clearly asked. He doesn't have any information about the situation in garrison. We are having the next witness who is called to rebut the evidence in that respect. This witness is called for three issues only, and none of them has anything to do with the situation in garrison in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I just ask the witness to remove his headphones for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the witness speak and understand English then?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] My English is not very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What do we make of that. I'll be very brief. Mr. Lisinovic, can you remove your earphones, please, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Clearly the witness speaks some English so he should be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we just -- just for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, before we ask the witness to be excused, Mr. Demirdjian, on the face of it, it seems that Mr. Zecevic's point is sound. Is this something that -- where you insist on proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the very next thing I'm about to say I don't want to say it in front of the witness not to affect his testimony in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, would the usher please escort the witness outside the court briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I apologise for not replying immediately, but my very answer to your question would impact in some way what the witness will say next. Mr. Zecevic has obviously read Mr. Lisinovic's statement, and at paragraph 12 the witness does discuss this relationship through his interaction with Mr. Jeftic. Now, Mr. Jeftic was a captain in the garrison, security officer. Mr. Lisinovic had the occasion to interact with him. It may be that the witness needs to be refreshed. I'm not going to try to refresh his memory right now. I'm just trying to get to the answer without refreshing his memory at this time. So I do know that he can answer that question. That's why I'm insisting at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, that is not the point, Your Honour. You see, the witness is called to testify about three issues only. The contents of his statements is not an issue over here. He has to testify what was -- what was the decision of the Trial Chamber is this witness is testifying on three issues only. Not about his general knowledge or the contents of his statement. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, the issue itself goes to the core of which units were in power in Doboj and who is about to take over the town. Now the relation between Mr. Hadzic and Stankovic goes to the heart of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness, may I remind -- the witness is on the -- by your decision of 15th December, 2011, the witness, Mirza Lisinovic, was allowed to be called in a rebuttal on the following topics: The imminent attack on Doboj by non-Serb forces as a justification for the take-over by Serbs and the question who ordered that take-over. That's one. B, adjudicated fact 1267, an evidence that Bjelosevic was away from the CSB Doboj in May and June 1992 and the functioning of the CSB Doboj during that period. Therefore, I don't see how this situation and the -- the situation within the garrison of Doboj reflects any of these -- is reflected in any of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Zecevic answered his own question. It's in relation to, in fact, who was in power and who controlled the army for the take-over of Doboj. They're claiming that it was a Muslim by the name of Cazim Hadzic. We're saying that it was a man by the name of Stankovic who was in charge of the garrison, so I think it goes straight to the heart of number (a), evidence that Doboj was on the verge of being attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was reminding myself of the -- our decision as Mr. Zecevic was on his feet, and the point about the functioning of CSB Doboj I suppose does come within subparagraph (a) of what is -- what we permitted to be led. So you may proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I guess we can call the witness back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lisinovic, let me go back to my question: Did you come to learn about the relationship between Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have exact information about their mutual relations. Why would I? However, as a person who was the commander of the defence of the town, Major Stankovic was the one who declared himself as the one in Doboj and the surrounding area. One could judge that by his public appearances when he spoke on the radio and how the citizens saw him and received him. I don't know how that came to happen, but, really, he was announced to be the commander of the defence of Doboj. He was not the commander of the barracks. But as for their relations, I couldn't talk about that because I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see Mr. Stankovic at the CSB building where you were working?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some visits when he came to the building where I work; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would other members of the army visit the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the military security. But there was also one type of these visits that, as policemen, we were not too happy about. And these were the visits of Mr. Predrag Kujundzic, who very frequently visited the police building. He was later charged with war crimes and also sentenced. His role was not quite clear over those months, whether he was a member of the military or a policeman or a military police, and whether the unit which was called Predo's Wolves was part of the military structure or not. We, as policemen, did not find that clear. And later on, the unit was involved in some unlawful acts and this man has been sentenced. This is what I can say about these other visits, if that was the thrust of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the Trial Chamber, during which time-period are we talking when we're dealing about the visits of Mr. Kujundzic and Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: We could say it was during three or four months before the 2nd of May, roughly, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just to wrap this up, in terms of frequency, how frequent would you say these visits were?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly. I couldn't say that these were daily or weekly visits. But we would meet from time to time. I worked on the same floor as the chief of the centre, so sometimes we would meet accidentally. We would see each other but there were probably also visits when I didn't see them or didn't know. So I couldn't really say what the frequency was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us about the army unit and you also now just mentioned Predo's Wolves. To your knowledge, there were paramilitary units in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which units, to your knowledge, were present in the Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I can talk about that on the basis of speculation and rumours that circulated among the citizens. We really couldn't see the units which would have any sort of symbols or insignia that would designate them as members of specific units. That did not exist. The uniforms that used to be the JNA uniforms were stripped of five-pointed star and they remained camouflage or olive-drab or whatever kind they were but without any specific insignia. There were stories going around, especially after the events in Bijeljina and so on, that units from Serbia, like Seselj's Men, the White Eagles, the Red Berets had arrived in Doboj. But, as I say, that was what the scared citizens talked among themselves. Whether there were such units stationed in the barracks, this is what somebody who was in the barracks could tell you. On the other hand, the local Serbs from Doboj were also concerned about units that may arrive from Croatia, and the area in the direction of the present day municipality of Usora was mentioned as the location where units such as the HOS and the ZNG units could have been stationed, but I took that to be only part of the speculation on part of the citizens that -- and stories going around, caused by fear, about what could happen. But whether it was really like that, and whether all that really existed, this is something I couldn't say, not having any evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. One of the first units you mentioned was the Seselj's Men and the White Eagles. Did you have any report on their present [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have specific reports. I just remember a situation. It seems to me that some property had gone missing. The sleepers from railway tracks between Doboj and Modrica had gone missing between Busletic and Kostajnica villages, and I think that there was this report about the wooden sleepers from the railway tracks that had gone missing and then stories were going around that the paramilitary units had taken that for their own needs, but whether that was based on anything, this is something I couldn't tell. Once again, it was just a rumour practically. I don't know, maybe the crime investigation section knew more about that, but investigations were not my line of work because this was a report on items that had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And one last question on this unit: Did you come to learn about where they were located or where they were stationed in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like the basis for that question because the witness, I believe, said that he didn't have any reports, didn't have any knowledge. It was just rumours. And now Mr. Demirdjian is asking where the unit was stationed. And the fact is that the witness doesn't know that the witness existed at all in the territory of Doboj at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it is a fair and non-leading question, and that the witness has heard of their presence. He could at least tell us if he knew where they were located. I don't see any harm in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, Mr. Lisinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that. I told you that I don't have any evidence or information about that. But judging by the report and items gone missing, Busletic and Kostajnica and Grapska villages were mentioned so that was the area. If the criminal investigation section investigated that, maybe they proved something about it, but as I told you, I really don't have any information about that, that anything like that was stationed or located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. These units that you mentioned to us earlier, including the Red Berets, and those rumours that you heard, you've described also the presence of the army and Predo's Wolves. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the ethnic composition of these units, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I can talk about Predo's Wolves because there is no doubt that such a unit did exist. These were the locals from Lipac, Suho Polje, Tekucica [phoen] villages. These are Serb-populated villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to weapon, were you aware of any locations where weapons were kept in the Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a specific question? Weapons by whom or -- I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't want to lead the witness. I'll let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's be slightly more specific, just to cover this a bit better. I'm talking about military equipment and military weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me whether there were weapons somewhere outside of the barracks that was available to anyone or what? I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: My apologies. Let me rephrase my questions [sic]. Were you aware of any locations where military equipment were kept in the Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the military equipment was held in military facilities. But during the last few months, the people thought that the military equipment was being transported to the Ozren mountain including a military hospital or military medical units, that everything was driven out to the settlements on the Ozren mountain outside of the town of Doboj, more or less to the places from which Predo's Wolves hailed which I mentioned. These were the stories going around and that was it. So the transportation of equipment, that would be not in any military facility, that was all that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you're telling us that these are stories. Did you know at the time whether this was an actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were frequent movements of military vehicles. There were military convoys transporting equipment. There were many convoys that were moving along these roads and going to these destinations. That is fact. But there were many movements of the army that was undoubtedly coming from Serbia. There were buses with licence plates that were full of troops and that were transiting through Doboj, together with military vehicles about which one couldn't tell where they belonged because, judging by the licence plates, you couldn't tell which town they were coming from. So that's what I could say about troops and equipment. It was quite intense, this migration of both troops and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And to close this chapter, what armed forces, if any, did you know that were present on the Doboj municipality belonging to the Muslim and Croat side?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about the military units, the Muslim and Croatian military units?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. In the municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in the Doboj municipality, there were no military units, at least that is my position, no Muslim or Croatian military units. There were reserve police stations that had been activated in the local communes, and that started in September 1991 and onwards. So there were these units that belonged to reserve police stations, together with their commanders, and these people were armed, but that was not the army. It is a fact that in certain places there were armed units as early as in September, but these were not army units. This was not the military. This is how I see things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you're talking about the reserve police station belonging to the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct, of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me move to the period slightly before the take-over. Can you tell us whether the structure you described in this morning, the structure of the CSB, whether that remained unchanged throughout the month of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of the Doboj CSB, which covers nine municipalities: Doboj, Brod, Samac, Derventa, Odzak, Modrica, Teslic, Maglaj and Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lisinovic, let me rephrase my question. I'm talking about the structure of the personnel within the CSB where you were working. Whether the composition, the composition of the personnel of the CSB remained unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yes. From the time when I started working at the centre, the chief, Hodzic, was killed in a car accident. He was succeeded by Klokic. The remaining structure formally stayed the same without any new personnel being appointed by decisions to specific assignments, but there was a disruption because people abandoned their posts during the months of, I don't know, March, April. So that, for example, Mr. Krnjic and Mr. Bilic stopped working. They stopped coming to work and had already been in Croatia a long time before the critical moment of the 2nd May in the evening. So two top officials. There were also many people who were on sick-leave - for example, Boro Kopcic, who was one of the duty operations officers - also stopped coming to work because of sick-leave, and then I had to cover him in some of the shifts. There were some new colleagues who had arrived from the municipal police stations in the Posavina area and they began working in Doboj. Now, as for specific names of those new colleagues, I couldn't really remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether you learned about the reasons why Mr. Krnjic and Bilic stopped coming to work?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were concerned about their own security. Namely, it happened that the chief of the municipal criminal investigation section of the police, Mato Krizic, was kidnapped from the street in the typical manner while he was coming to the work. The army did that, and they held him for a few days in some sort of isolation, we don't know where, and then they released him. And that influenced a number of people to stop living in Doboj, let alone come to work, and Krizic was the municipal chief of the criminal investigation section at the police station in Doboj. I think that was one of the reasons. And generally speaking, that was a period when people, believing that a war would break out, were leaving the area to go somewhere where they felt more secure and that included police chiefs and regular policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let's come to the take-over. Can you describe to us what you were doing on the 2nd of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: My superior, Mr. Blagojevic, summoned me on the 2nd of May, in the evening to be on duty, because Mr. Boro Kopcic, who was the duty operations officer, was on sick-leave at the time. So I reported for work beginning at 7.00 p.m., and I was supposed to work until 7.00 a.m. the next morning. That night was very stressful, critical dynamic. There were many calls we received. We were informed about roads that had been blocked. The trains were not going anymore. They were people who called us who were calling the municipal police number, 92, and then from the duty operations officers in police stations, mainly from the Doboj police station I would receive such news. So practically on the 2nd of May, the blockade of the town began during the day. There was no traffic anymore on the roads or on the railway. I was alone, as the duty officer on the second floor at the centre. Sometime around midnight, perhaps, I received a call from Tuzla, from a military officer from the barracks who said that on that stretch between Doboj and Tuzla, an army officer had been kidnapped. I cannot remember his name now. But I was trying to get in touch with the duty operations officer in the Doboj barracks so that they would go out on the ground because this was the jurisdiction of the military security. And while I was having this telephone conversation, three masked men entered my office. They were wearing those camouflage hats without any insignia, but they had -- you could see the places where their red stars had been - it were the emblems - and they arrested me. And so I stopped working for the police. It could have happened between midnight and 1.00 a.m., roughly. I don't know if you want to hear the details about everything else that was going on, but that's what I could tell you about that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you some follow-up questions about what you just told us: Through these telephone calls that you were receiving, were you informed of any imminent threat of an attack on the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing was formally announced. There were no announcements or statements to the effect that that would happen. It was sudden for us. Why would I be there if I knew that I could get killed at night or be imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on that day, did you hear of any order issued by the army, by the garrison, Doboj, in relation to the security situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: About the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Not about the attack, but there were some pacifying statements addressing the citizens by the head of the municipality and the top army officers to the effect that there would be no war. There were some announcement to that effect on the previous day, that there was no war, that there was no conflict. But as for any formal orders to attack or anything like that, that did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now you told us that you were taken by these men in balaclavas. Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one among them who was the leader of the group said that I should go on sitting there and answering the phone and I should say that everything is regular, that there are no problems, that we are working, and so on and so forth. He ordered the other two, that if I said anything to the contrary that they were allowed to kill me. Before that, they took away my official pistol which I had on me. I had to stand against the wall and they frisked me and they took it away. So I sat there for another half an hour. I could hear that they were breaking the doors and safes down the corridor. Then they took me to the ground floor and the entire municipal police team had been arrested. They were located on the floor below me. Maybe five or six men in total. We were all beaten up there. Luckily I had a long leather jacket which protected me quite well, but it broke in several places. I tried to block the strikes with my arms but then I sustained some injuries on my arms. Then we were transported to the district prison. It is the adjacent building. You just needed to go through the yard and the same thing happened again because people who were in charge of receiving us were there. So after being beaten, I was placed in cell number 10 on the -- the upper floor of the municipal prison. Before us, the policemen, two prison guards, had already been placed in these rooms. One of them was in room 10. It was Meho Alicic. He had been beaten really bad. But they left him handcuffed so that by defending himself, he squeezed his arms and he asked me to loosen the handcuffs a little bit for him. And he had the key in his pocket because he was a prison guard. So I loosened it. I washed his face a little bit and assisted him. And I'm not sure in what condition he would have been in the morning if he had remained alone in the cell. Alicic was released the following day. He left. And I don't know what happened to him. On the following day they started bringing people to the prison. As they called on people to report themselves for work obligation, the people who were coming to work were then classified. A gentleman who came to my cell, the manager of the Bosanka factory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- told me that he had arrived for work, and once he had arrived to the gate, he was brought to the prison. He was also beaten up. And then they also brought Slavko Duspara, who was also another manager from the same company. Then they brought some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, it appears that the conduct of this testimony is quite outside the scope of rebuttal evidence that this witness -- or the Prosecution is permitted to lead it at this point. Because we are hearing the same story about the Doboj which we heard during the general case. I would -- I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to intervene and ask Mr. Demirdjian to focus the testimony of the witness to the three issues that he was called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will refrain my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Lisinovic, it seems that you have speeded up again. I would remind you of what the interpreters has asked a while ago for you to slow down so that they can keep up. There was the -- when you had indicated the name of the -- a certain factory, the witness -- the interpreter hadn't gotten it and asked you to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, the name of the manager of the Bosanska factory was not recorded. If you could repeat his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for my speed. I was talking about the juice factory Bosanka in Doboj, and the managers were the Rafael Romic and Slavko Duspara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How long were you detained, Mr. Lisinovic, in the prison? How long were you --

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any translation. Two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And did you know the exact date of your release?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: On the afternoon of the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If there's no objection to this, I'm not going to show the log-book of this again if Mr. Zecevic agrees that this witness was detained until the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do not dispute that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lisinovic, once you were released, did you return to your position in CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, when I was taken out of the cell for a short period of time and told that I would go home, I was told that the first next working day, that was the Monday, the 18th of May, I should report to the chief of the centre, Andrija Bjelosevic. That was the instruction that I received. I was told to go home and then to report to the chief Bjelosevic on the Monday. I did so. I reported at the CSB at the gate and the reception area where citizens normally came. They let me go upstairs to the second floor because I said I had an arrangement with the chief. I did not know the person who was working at the gate on that morning. He was a new employee. First, I went to the chief's secretary office, where I stayed for a while, and then I went to Chief Bjelosevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in the chief's secretary office, was the secretary there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Bjelosevic immediately when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I was with his secretary for a short time. Since the corridor door was open, Mr. Blagojevic appeared as well. He was my superior. We greeted each others [as interpreted] but he didn't stay long. He went away, after which I entered Chief Bjelosevic's office. We spent about ten minutes talking. He received me and he said that he was not pleased with what had happened with me, but he said that maybe I would have faired much worse had I been in my flat because I had a police uniform and other equipment and that perhaps somebody could even have killed me. So it was better for me to have been in the prison. Then he asked me about my father, since he knew him, because my father had a war time assignment as a reserve officer. He was about 60 years of age and he was working at the municipal TO staff or something like that. That's how Bjelosevic knew him. He asked me if it was possible for me to influence my native village of Kotorsko to surrender weapons in order to avoid the destiny of other villages. I told him that there were other elders in that village of mine that they should appeal to, that I wasn't involved in these kind of things. Then police officer Vojo Maric [as interpreted] came. He was in charge of these kind of operations. We went to my office. I handed over the keys to the safe to him, and with that, my police career ended. Mr. Bjelosevic told me that the time has come, that only Serbs could work in the police, that I should go home and wait to see what would happen. I lived some 3- or 400 metres from the police, and then on the 27th of July, I, myself, my wife, my child, and a group of other people were exchanged, and we headed towards Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now let me backtrack a little bit. When you arrived at the secretary's office, did you know what Mr. Bjelosevic was doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't know that. How would I have known that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have to wait for a period of time or did you go into his office immediately?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I sat with his secretary for a few minutes, up to five minutes. I don't know. I didn't enter immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there anyone else in his office when you entered his office?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: A stranger came out who had been with him, but only the chief and Vojo Maric were there when I entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you told us that he asked you whether you can influence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Demirdjian, is this convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lisinovic, we are about to take our first break. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lisinovic, I just want a couple of clarifications. First of all, in the transcript at page 30, line 24, you gave us the name of a police officer who took your keys to the safe. Could you tell us his name again?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Vojo Naric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a part of your answer that was not recorded and it was in relation to your discussion with Mr. Bjelosevic. You were talking about influencing your village Kotorsko. Could you please repeat that part of your answer? This is at page 30, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic asked me if I could influence my fellow villagers of Kotorsko in surrendering their weapons in order to avoid the fate that befell the village of Grabska. That was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know whether other policemen went through the same procedure you went through during that time, when you were called into Mr. Bjelosevic's office?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Did the chief receive other policemen following their release from the prison? No. I haven't heard of any such case. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, did other non-Serb police officers return to work, CSB Doboj, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not a single policeman who was not a Serb worked after the 1st of May there. That's to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting and until your exchange on the 27th of July, could you briefly tell the Court what you were doing? What were your activities?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I spent time in my flat. It's a high-rise building of 16 storeys. I lived on the eighth storey. My wife continued to work in her company for a few days more, but then she stopped working as well. We spent all our time in our flat with our child. And the allowed period of time for movement in town was from 8.00 until 11.00 in the morning for people to do their shopping and get groceries, et cetera, but that was mostly done by my wife. I didn't venture out into the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you were limited to staying at home?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the permitted period of movement time for civilians was what I said, and outside that period, it was dangerous to walk in the streets, and I refrained from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lisinovic, did you know a man in Doboj by the name of Mile Bosnjak.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: There was a police officer who had already been retired before the 2nd of May. I know a retired police officer by the name of Bosnjak. But that's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did he retire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I think two or three years prior to these events in Doboj. It may have been in 1988 or 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did he hold any position prior to retiring?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he did. I think he was a regular police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just to clarify this, your answers says: "I know a retired police officer by the name of Bosnjak," and there's a caret there. Did you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So before the war, did he know his full name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go much into details, his personal details. But I think his full name was Mile Bosnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, sir, you told us that you were released on the 27th of July. You were -- sorry. You were exchanged on the 27th of July and you ended up in Tesanj. What did you do exactly in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: The following day, I inquired in Tesanj whether there were any Doboj police structures, but that it was located in Bregovica [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Alibegovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the neighbourhood that belonged to the municipality of Doboj before the war, but now it was gravitating more to Tesanj. It was mostly populated by Croats, and there were a few Bosniaks. And that is where the relocated Doboj police station was, and I reported there the next day, on the 28th of July, to start working as a policeman. However, after some 15 or 20 days, I received from the Doboj Municipal Defence Staff, again, in a new location, an assignment to the Defence Staff of Doboj as the assistant commander for security. And I stayed in that position from August until approximately mid-1993. Then, in May 1993, I returned to police force and that is where I worked, nowadays as well. So I have a few months during war-time-period when I was not working for the police, but, rather, for the military because that was my war time assignment, and physically, I was, all the time, at this relocated station. There was another station in Brijesnica which is the part of Doboj that faces Gracanica. So there were two police stations because Doboj, as a result of war, was split into two. And the end of war found me at the Brijesnica police station as its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, as a result of a request from the Defence, we obtained your personnel file, and we have seen several documents about your appointments. And there's one document that I would like to show on the screen. It is at tab 10. 65 ter 20411.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, it is 65 ter 20411.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- oh, no. Hang on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's go to, in the B/C/S, page 12. And in the English, I believe it's page 3. All right. So, yes. English, if we could move to page -- I believe it is page 3. Can we go to the next page in the English. Next one again. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate confirming the participation in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of the armed forces and the periods of time spent as part of that engagement. The purpose of this is to calculate the pensionable service because war-time service is calculated on a -- on the basis of a different formula. It's an accelerated rate of service, and it was issued by the responsible or competent administration in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, below the title: "Confirmation," we see your name. And under number 1, we see: "VJ 32104/4." And we see a period of time between the 1st of April and the 3rd of May, 1992. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the period from the 1st of April when the state of war was proclaimed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a war time assignment commenced on that date. And I worked there until the 3rd of May, 1992. Then there was a gap until the 27th of July, the time which I spent either in prison or in my flat. And then the second period goes to the end of the war in 1995. This designation VJ 32104 is the designation of the Doboj police station, and as such it is entered in the military booklet. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to comply with your request and provide my military booklet because I couldn't go home where it is. But I gave it to you yesterday, and it says Doboj SJB, and this is how it is registered in the Defence documents. The official term "milicija" was changed into "police" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in August of 1993, and there was a decree law issued that those who participated in war, whether they be military personnel or members of the police, should be calculated as the time spent in war assignment, so that due to that, I don't have any gaps in my service -- or, rather, that was no gap in my employment, although there was a period of time when I was not working for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what I'm interested in is this period of time from the 1st of April to the 3rd of May. Could you just clarify to us, because it says here "time served as a member of the armed forces of BiH." Where were you working in this period?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I was only a police officer. I don't know, however, how the defence organs or the Ministry of Defence treated that, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say you were a police officer, as you've said before, this is in the CSB building in Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Until the 7th of -- 27th of July, when I started working in Alibegovci, where a new police station was set up. But before that period, I wasn't working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we do have your military booklet just to connect this digit that you have there. And it's 65 ter 20413.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pull that up? It's at tab 12. On the B/C/S version, can we go -- we only have a B/C/S version, Your Honours. We'll ask for a translation. Can we go to -- well, this is the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We see your name and your particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please. And can we zoom to the top right corner of this booklet. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now we could see the code that we just saw on the previous document. And next to it, it does -- it indicates the unit you were working for. And which -- what does it say on the -- next to your code?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: SJB, which is the public security station, Doboj. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that's from the period starting on the 27th of July. And if we look at the two rows below, there's the same codes from the 1st of April [Realtime transcript read in error "July"]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you told us there was a decree that was adopted in 1993 which made it that the armed forces of BiH include both the army and the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Demirdjian. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just I'm confused now. 38:2. And if we look at the two rows there's the same code which says "from the 1st of July"; is that right? I think you said "1st of April."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I did say 1st of April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It should be corrected then in the transcript. 38:2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, I did say from the 1st of April, 1992, until the 3rd of May. Yeah, until the 3rd of May. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now I didn't have the chance to show you this document. We just located it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we pull up tab 11, which is 65 ter 20412.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And -- yes. In the B/C/S version, and also in the English version, both page 1, can we zoom into Article 1. This is: "A decree with the force of law on changes and amendments to the decree with the force of law on armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, can you look at Article 1, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this the disposition of the law that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you read in the quotation marks where it says: "Armed forces during the time of martial law are comprised of: Army and police of the Ministry of Interior ...," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That means that during the state of war, the armed forces are made up of the army and the police of the Ministry of Interior, as well as the units of security in enterprises and other legal persons and units of customs services designated by the Supreme Command of the armed forces. That is what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Therefore, although you were working for the police, as a result of this decree, you were considered to be as part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object at this point because this document is from 1993. It's not related to period of indictment. So why [indiscernible] this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is in relation to the status of the witness when he was arrested, and I think it is relevant. And maybe he could tell us how this applied in his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- is -- I suppose he would have to -- the question would be to what extent is this 1993 edict back referenced to the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's the substance of my objection, because if you look at the document which has been presented to the witness, there is a number of decrees from 1993 which regulated his status. So if the Prosecutor wants to determine what his status was in 1992, then he should present him with these decrees because the decree changed his status from the one in 1992. The decrees in 1992 which determined his status in 1992 have been changed with this decree. So if we want to see what his status was and what legal basis for it was in 1992 then he should be shown the decrees from Article 1 in the preamble which have been changed by this decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ignoring, Mr. Krgovic, the evidence that you have just given, the relevant issue, it seems to me, is whether the witness is able to -- well, whether counsel - Mr. Demirdjian, who is on his feet - is able to elicit from the witness the equivalent decree for the relevant period. If he isn't, then Mr. Krgovic's objection clearly must be upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lisinovic, when you referred earlier to a decree in 1993 changing the status, was this the wording you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that the issue of determining the exact status that I had during the war or immediately preceding that? I said that this decree law was adopted in order to equal the position of policemen with the status of members of the army, in terms of their status as persons who were involved in the war. I have around 15 documents which I enclosed that explain day by day my movement during the war and the status which I had. I was only a policeman up until the 15th of August, or, I'm not sure what date, mid-August 1992, when, by the decision of the Ministry of Defence, I was transferred to the Municipal Defence Staff and I was there until 1993. After that, I was only a policeman. These decrees were passed later, and my military booklet was drawn up and issued in 1995. The first certificate that I have is also dating from 1995. So it's all after the fact. But I cannot offer you anything else. I have given you all the decisions on my assignments, from the Republican Secretariat and from local units and later. So everything is covered, all the assignments which I had. There is nothing that is in dispute and I was also a policeman except for the engagement from August 1992 until the May of 1993. Now I cannot really go into the analysis of legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I think you've clarified it to the Trial Chamber. The certificate, the first one that we showed, was dating from -- it says here 1995. But it is correct that it was 2005; is that right? The certificate indicating your time as a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the first document which you showed me dates from 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2005; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: So that was issued in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. So when those documents were drafted --

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: It's the military booklet that was issued in 1995. Only the military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. So these documents were created after the 1993 decree was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the limited purpose of establishing the status of the witness in 1992, I would ask that his military booklet, the certificate I showed early, as well as the gazette we're looking at right now be admitted in evidence and, again, just to establish the purpose of his status between 1st of April and the 3rd of May 1992. I don't know if there are any challenges from the Defence about his status, but, otherwise, I think to support his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not object. We will be using the same documents in the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Zupljanin's Defence has a somewhat different position. These documents do not show the status he had in 1992, so they are irrelevant because they were drawn up later on the basis of regulations which were adopted in 1993. If we are to determine his status in 1992, we should bring the documents from 1992 and the military booklet from 1992, which existed then and look at the decrees which were changed by the decree dating from 1993 so that we could see how his status was regulated in 1992. And for that purpose, these documents cannot be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- it seems notwithstanding what Mr. Zecevic has indicated about his intention to use the same documents, there is no problem about him using them in the way that you have, but I do have a problem with exhibiting them along the lines of Mr. Krgovic's objection. And it seems to me that the relevant evidence which the witness has given is sufficient and that to admit these as items of evidence would inject a measure of confusion which would be totally unnecessary. But, as I said, that doesn't prohibit you -- you from -- you've used them, and Mr. Zecevic said that he would do likewise, and I don't know that we would be assisted by formally exhibiting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I intervene here only because it goes to a wider issue than just what has been raised with this witness. Your Honours will know that there is an issue which is still a live issue on the subject of various motions in respect of the status of some of the named victims on the indictment, and various documents have been received from the authorities concerned. It is our contention that it is possible that an explanation for what, on the face it, appears to be a contradictory aspect to these victims can be explained by decrees such as this. And it's certainly a matter that is going to be the subject of argument. And as Mr. Zecevic has said, that he proposes to use these documents in any event, Your Honours, it seems to me that they probably should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that now I have a problem. Because my understanding was that this document goes to the credibility of the witness and that -- that they were offered by Mr. Demirdjian for the sole purposes of establishing his status in between certain dates which are relevant to this indictment. And on that, I don't have a problem. But now, if Ms. Korner wants to use them to further another aspect of these documents and as a basis of the theory, and may I say a wrong one, as a matter of fact, then I certainly do have a problem with that, and I would oppose that this document be admitted on -- on basis of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is must have occurred to -- the reason when this witness explained -- it became apparent that it had a knock-on effect. It certainly goes further than his credibility. But, Your Honour, I'm not sure what -- what exactly it is that Mr. Zecevic is now suggesting. He is going to refer to these documents when, in cross-examination it's clear these documents, if they're going to be referred to by both parties in some form or another, have to be exhibited, the use to which they may be put at later stage is a question of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I listen to the Prosecution reflecting on the -- what seems to be a new twist on the rule that a party is not expected to introduce contradiction or confusion in its own case, but let me -- we'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded that these documents should be admitted in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just one final question, Mr. Lisinovic, before I conclude: It is your position that during the month of April 1992, you worked throughout that time at CSB Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA LISINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would kindly ask that our cross-examination be deferred until tomorrow morning. Your Honours, the reasons are the following: We interviewed this witness only on -- on January 6th, last Friday, and the transcript was -- the transcript of the interview was done only on the 8th of January because in the -- in between was the Orthodox Christmas, as you know. Orthodox Christmas, yes. And we had a number of documents, some 21 documents, which we wanted to show to the witness in anticipation of the witness's testimony. However, 85 per cent, of course, of them were not translated because we received them only on Friday last week. Now, we are -- at this point we are able to prioritise our request for translations because I would need only two or three documents, and I believe that tomorrow morning we have that document with the help of the CLSS which will enable me to finish my cross-examination fairly quickly within, I believe, one session. I think it is just for the practical purposes I'm asking for that my cross-examination be deferred until tomorrow morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Notwithstanding the issue of translations, I would like to inform the Chamber that the witnesses needs to fly back tomorrow afternoon. He has already expressed that wish because of commitments having regard of his position back in Bosnia. That's number one. Number two, I believe that Mr. Krgovic also has some questions to ask, so whether it would be possible for him to conduct his cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to ask that, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.
